sample_unit: discharge letters (72 learning objectives; 787 sentences in patient letters)

links.outcome: Patient-centricity and readability of GPT-4 patient letters versus discharge letters
links.effect: Patient letters had fewer medical terms (132/860, 15.3% vs 165/273, 60.4%), fewer abbreviations (43/860, 5% vs 49/273, 17.9%), and more explanations of medical terms (121/131, 92.4% vs 0/165, 0%).
links.quote: Compared with discharge letters, they included fewer medical terms (132/860, 15.3%, vs 165/273, 60/4%), fewer abbreviations (43/860, 5%, vs 49/273, 17.9%), and more explanations of medical terms (121/131, 92.4%, vs 0/165, 0%).

links.outcome: Omission of safety-relevant information and medical errors in GPT-4 patient letters
links.effect: 56/72 (78%) learning objectives addressed; 11/72 (15%) omitted in most letters; medical errors in 31/787 sentences (3.9%).
links.quote: Medical errors were found in a small proportion of sentences (31/787, 3.9%).

unlisted_practices: Prompt engineering to improve completeness of transformed discharge letters

screen.reason: The study empirically evaluates GPT-4's performance and safety (omissions, medical errors, readability) in transforming synthetic discharge letters into patient-centered letters, but does not test a specific deployment safeguard or compare outcomes with/without a deployment practice.
